newsitem.title: USA: MINN. STADIUM DEBATE MAY REACH NOVEMBER BALLOT.
newsitem.headline: MINN. STADIUM DEBATE MAY REACH NOVEMBER BALLOT.

text.p: Minnesota lawmakers studied plans for a new ballpark and hockey arena Wednesday as Minneapolis election officials sought to determine if the public debate over financing professional sports facilities will make the November ballot.

A legislative task force Wednesday reviewed financing plans for a proposed Minnesota Twins ballpark on the Minneapolis riverfront and toured the site selected for a new downtown St. Paul arena to house the state's future National Hockey League expansion team.

At the same time, Minneapolis election officials reviewed a petition from political group Progressive Minnesota which wants a charter amendment on the citywide ballot that would require a popular vote for public contributions to sports facilities exceeding $10 million.
Minneapolis election board director Joyce Swadner anticipates completing a review of the petition by 1900 EDT on Thursday, but said Wednesday it did not appear to meet requirements.

Only 2,018 of the 4,500 signatures checked as of Tuesday afternoon were valid, Swadner said. The group stated that it had submitted about 10,100 signatures and needs 8,155 to make the ballot, she noted.
Minnesota law allows a petitioner 10 days to submit more signatures. If a petition remains insufficient at that point it is dead, Swadner said.

If lawmakers approve a stadium plan before the general election, the petition could be moot for the ballpark, but would still set an important precedent, Progressive Minnesota spokeswoman Jennifer Smith said.
"We think there are higher priorities, let the voters decide, not the politicians," Smith said.
The legislative task force does not expect to vote on funding proposals for at least two weeks, said Sen. Keith Langseth, D-Glyndon, who co-chairs the group.
"Assuming (the session) is in late September, if we came up with a specific proposal by the middle of September, that would probably fit the schedule," Langseth said.
Twins owner Carl Pohlad has received permission to explore the possible sale and relocation of the team and said he would pursue other options if the franchise does not receive a new ballpark.
A new retractable roof ballpark is projected to cost more than $400 million. The Minnesota Vikings, a co-tenant in the Metrodome with the Twins, want the stadium talks to include them.
Lawmakers have also decided to review the St. Paul arena project, for which Gov. Arne Carlson pledged $65 million of state bonds in the capital spending package next year.

Minneapolis City Council on Friday approved the riverfront site near the Metrodome with public and private financing estimated at $54 million to $58 million, said Amy Phenix, spokeswoman for Minneapolis Mayor Sharon Sayles Belton.
The site includes active businesses, old grain elevators and railroad tracks that would be cleared for about $8.6 million, Phenix said.

A $22 million revenue bond-financed parking ramp would be constructed on the site, which includes nearly $10 million of land donated by Minneapolis, Hennepin County and the private sector, Phenix said.
